subject: Psychiatry
topic: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor Hypertensive Crisis Management
stem: A 44-year-old woman with treatment-resistant depression is brought to the emergency department with a sudden, excruciating, pounding occipital headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, and chest tightness that began 45 minutes after attending an artisan wine and cheese tasting party. Her home medications include phenelzine, which she has been taking for 6 months with significant improvement in her depressive symptoms. On physical examination, the patient is pale, trembling, and profusely diaphoretic. Her blood pressure is 224/128 mm Hg, heart rate is 122/min, and respirations are 22/min. Physical examination reveals widely dilated pupils that are reactive to light, jugular venous distension, and cold, clammy extremities. Cardiovascular examination reveals a hyperdynamic precordium with an audible S4 gallop and no murmurs. Neurological examination demonstrates no focal weakness, but mild bilateral hand tremors are present. An electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus tachycardia with diffuse ST-segment depressions in the lateral precordial leads. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic agent to reduce this patient's blood pressure?

options.text: Intravenous phentolamine mesylate or sodium nitroprusside
options.explanation: This patient is experiencing an acute HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS ("cheese reaction") resulting from an interaction between a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI, phenelzine) and dietary tyramine. Monoamine oxidase-A in the gastrointestinal mucosa and liver normally metabolizes dietary tyramine into inactive metabolites. When irreversible MAOIs block this enzymatic degradation, ingested tyramine from fermented, aged foods (such as aged cheeses, cured meats, red wine, or draft beer) enters the systemic circulation intact. Tyramine is an indirect sympathomimetic amine: it is taken up into presynaptic adrenergic terminals via the norepinephrine transporter (NET) and displaces massive stores of norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft. This produces an explosive sympathetic adrenergic storm, causing extreme peripheral vasoconstriction, malignant hypertension (BP 224/128 mm Hg), severe occipital headache, diaphoresis, and myocardial ischemia. The treatment of choice is an INTRAVENOUS ALPHA-ADRENERGIC RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST—specifically PHENTOLAMINE (a competitive non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptor blocker) or intravenous vasodilators like SODIUM NITROPRUSSIDE or labetalol. Crucially, pure beta-blockers (like propranolol) must be avoided, as uninhibited alpha-adrenergic stimulation can paradoxically worsen vasoconstriction and hypertension.

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol tartrate bolus monotherapy
options.explanation: Pure beta-blockers leave alpha-1 adrenergic receptors unopposed, precipitating severe paradoxical worsening of peripheral vasoconstriction and malignant hypertension.

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine immediate-release capsule
options.explanation: Sublingual immediate-release nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous drops in blood pressure and is associated with stroke and myocardial infarction.

options.text: Oral sumatriptan tablet for acute migraine relief
options.explanation: Sumatriptan causes coronary and cranial vasoconstriction and has serotonergic properties; giving it in this setting risks catastrophic cerebral infarction.

options.text: Continuous intravenous epinephrine infusion
options.explanation: Epinephrine is a potent alpha- and beta-agonist that will escalate blood pressure to lethal levels and trigger aortic dissection or intracerebral hemorrhage.

explanation: This patient is experiencing an acute HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS ("cheese reaction") resulting from an interaction between a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI, phenelzine) and dietary tyramine. Monoamine oxidase-A in the gastrointestinal mucosa and liver normally metabolizes dietary tyramine into inactive metabolites. When irreversible MAOIs block this enzymatic degradation, ingested tyramine from fermented, aged foods (such as aged cheeses, cured meats, red wine, or draft beer) enters the systemic circulation intact. Tyramine is an indirect sympathomimetic amine: it is taken up into presynaptic adrenergic terminals via the norepinephrine transporter (NET) and displaces massive stores of norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft. This produces an explosive sympathetic adrenergic storm, causing extreme peripheral vasoconstriction, malignant hypertension (BP 224/128 mm Hg), severe occipital headache, diaphoresis, and myocardial ischemia. The treatment of choice is an INTRAVENOUS ALPHA-ADRENERGIC RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST—specifically PHENTOLAMINE (a competitive non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptor blocker) or intravenous vasodilators like SODIUM NITROPRUSSIDE or labetalol. Crucially, pure beta-blockers (like propranolol) must be avoided, as uninhibited alpha-adrenergic stimulation can paradoxically worsen vasoconstriction and hypertension. Manifestations: Severe occipital headache, profuse sweating, dilated pupils, and MALIGNANT HYPERTENSION (BP > 180/120 mm Hg) risking stroke or aortic dissection. TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS PHENTOLAMINE (non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic blocker) or NITROPRUSSIDE.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Clozapine-Induced Agranulocytosis Monitoring and Management
stem: A 36-year-old man with refractory schizophrenia has been treated with oral clozapine for the past 14 weeks after failing trials of olanzapine and risperidone. His auditory hallucinations have resolved, and he has reintegrated well with his family. Today, he presents to the outpatient clinic for his routine scheduled laboratory monitoring. He reports feeling mildly fatigued and notes a sore throat and low-grade chills that began yesterday. On physical examination, his temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg, heart rate is 98/min, and respirations are 16/min. Examination of the oropharynx reveals mild erythema and tonsillar pillar injection without purulent exudates; there is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examinations are unremarkable. Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, platelet count 240,000/mm³, and white blood cell count 1,200/mm³ with 18% segmented neutrophils and 2% bands (calculated absolute neutrophil count [ANC] 240/mm³). Baseline ANC prior to clozapine initiation was 4,200/mm³. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose by 50% and repeat the complete blood count in 48 hours
options.explanation: Dose reduction is completely inadequate; continuing clozapine in the setting of ANC 240/mm³ leads to fulminant septic shock and death.

options.text: Immediately and permanently discontinue clozapine, admit to the hospital for reverse isolation, and initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage
options.explanation: This patient presents with clozapine-induced agranulocytosis complicated by neutropenic fever (sore throat, fever 38.4°C, and ANC 240/mm³). Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and suicidal behavior, but its clinical utility is constrained by a ~1% risk of potentially fatal idiosyncratic agranulocytosis (typically peaking during the first 3 to 6 months of treatment). Strict regulatory registries mandate baseline and serial ANC monitoring: weekly for the first 6 months, every 2 weeks for months 6 to 12, and monthly thereafter. When severe neutropenia occurs (ANC < 1,000/mm³, and particularly agranulocytosis with ANC < 500/mm³), the standard of care dictates: (1) IMMEDIATE AND PERMANENT DISCONTINUATION OF CLOZAPINE; (2) Immediate inpatient hospital admission with protective reverse isolation precautions; (3) Urgent infectious workup (blood and urine cultures) and initiation of empiric broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., cefepime); and (4) Consideration of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF/filgrastim). Because of high recurrence and mortality, patients who develop clozapine agranulocytosis must NEVER BE RECHALLENGED with clozapine in the future.

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin-clavulanate outpatient therapy and continue clozapine at the current dose
options.explanation: Outpatient oral antibiotics are contraindicated for neutropenic fever with agranulocytosis; inpatient hospitalization and immediate drug cessation are required.

options.text: Switch clozapine to high-dose carbamazepine to manage both psychosis and mood stability
options.explanation: Carbamazepine also causes bone marrow suppression and aplastic anemia, which is synergistic with clozapine toxicity and strictly contraindicated.

options.text: Administer intramuscular benztropine and continue close observation in the clinic
options.explanation: Benztropine treats extrapyramidal symptoms; it has zero efficacy in reversing life-threatening clozapine-induced neutrophil depletion.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Acute Catatonia Diagnosis and Lorazepam Challenge
stem: A 29-year-old woman with a history of bipolar I disorder is brought to the psychiatric emergency service by her parents because of a profound, sudden change in behavior over the past 48 hours. Her parents report that she stopped speaking, refused all food and water, and has remained motionless in her bedroom. On physical examination, the patient is awake with her eyes open, staring blankly ahead into space. She does not speak or respond to verbal questions (mutism) and makes no spontaneous movements. When the examiner elevates her right arm above her head, she maintains this unnatural, awkward posture indefinitely against gravity without fatigue (catalepsy). When the examiner attempts to passively bend her elbow, there is smooth, plastic resistance reminiscent of bending a candle (waxy flexibility). When instructed to open her mouth, she clamps her teeth shut tighter (negativism). Her vital signs are: temperature 37.1°C (98.8°F), blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, and respirations 16/min. Comprehensive laboratory workup, urine drug screen, and non-contrast head CT scan are all completely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for this patient?

options.text: Administer intramuscular haloperidol to manage severe psychotic immobility
options.explanation: Antipsychotics such as haloperidol are strictly contraindicated in acute catatonia because dopamine D2 blockade markedly worsens catatonic symptoms and precipitates fatal malignant catatonia or NMS.

options.text: Immediate involuntary civil commitment for stereotactic cingulotomy
options.explanation: Psychosurgical procedures are historical or reserved for extreme refractory OCD; catatonia responds rapidly to medical therapy with lorazepam or ECT.

options.text: Administer an intravenous lorazepam challenge test
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute CATATONIA complicating bipolar disorder. Catatonia is a severe psychomotor syndrome characterized by a cluster of motor, behavioral, and vocal abnormalities. Classic clinical signs include: (1) Mutism (minimal or absent verbal response); (2) Stupor (unresponsiveness to external stimuli); (3) Catalepsy (passive induction of a posture held against gravity); (4) Waxy flexibility (initial slight resistance followed by yielding to passive repositioning); and (5) Negativism (active resistance to instructions or movement). The gold-standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic intervention is the INTRAVENOUS LORAZEPAM CHALLENGE TEST. Administering 1 to 2 mg of IV lorazepam typically produces dramatic, rapid resolution or significant improvement of catatonic signs within 10 to 15 minutes, conclusively confirming the diagnosis. If positive, the patient is started on scheduled standing lorazepam (often requiring high daily doses, 6 to 16 mg/day). If catatonia is refractory to benzodiazepines, or if malignant catatonia develops (autonomic instability, hyperthermia), ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY (ECT) is the definitive, life-saving treatment of choice. CRITICAL WARNING: Antipsychotic medications must be strictly avoided, as they exacerbate catatonia and trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

options.text: Initiate oral lithium carbonate titration with daily therapeutic serum levels
options.explanation: Lithium is a maintenance mood stabilizer that takes 1 to 2 weeks to titrate; it does not treat acute catatonic mutism or dehydration.

options.text: Perform an emergency diagnostic lumbar puncture to rule out viral encephalitis
options.explanation: With a normal head CT, normal vital signs, absent fever, and classic waxy flexibility and catalepsy, lorazepam challenge is the immediate priority.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Acute Severe Agitation in the Emergency Department
stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after being found yelling incoherently, smashing shop windows, and threatening bystanders with a broken glass bottle. In the triage area, the patient is pacing frantically, screaming profanities, and claiming that government agents are trying to steal his organs. The emergency physician and nursing staff attempt verbal de-escalation in a calm, quiet room from a safe distance, but the patient becomes increasingly combative. He suddenly picks up a metal intravenous pole, brandishes it as a weapon, and advances aggressively toward a nurse, shouting that he will kill anyone who approaches him. Hospital security officers physically restrain the patient to the floor to prevent immediate physical harm to staff. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention for this patient?

options.text: Simultaneous intramuscular administration of olanzapine and intramuscular lorazepam
options.explanation: Co-administering intramuscular olanzapine and an intramuscular benzodiazepine carries an FDA black-box warning for severe synergistic cardiorespiratory depression, profound hypotension, and death.

options.text: Prescription of oral liquid risperidone and request that the patient swallow it voluntarily
options.explanation: Oral medications are appropriate for cooperative patients; offering oral tablets to an actively combative, violent patient brandishing a weapon is impossible and unsafe.

options.text: Subcutaneous injection of regular insulin and dextrose to calm adrenergic hyperactivity
options.explanation: Administering insulin to an agitated patient without documented diabetic ketoacidosis causes life-threatening hypoglycemia and brain injury.

options.text: Intramuscular administration of haloperidol combined with intramuscular lorazepam
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute, severe, violent agitation with active assaultive behavior that poses an immediate, life-threatening danger to himself and medical staff. While the initial preferred approach to any agitated patient is verbal de-escalation in a safe, non-threatening environment, verbal de-escalation has completely failed. When a patient demonstrates active physical violence or weapon brandishing, immediate rapid chemical sedation is necessary to prevent severe injury. The most widely established, effective, and safe rapid-acting parenteral regimen is the combination of an INTRAMUSCULAR HIGH-POTENCY FIRST-GENERATION ANTIPSYCHOTIC (haloperidol 5 mg) AND AN INTRAMUSCULAR BENZODIAZEPINE (lorazepam 2 mg)—frequently referred to as the "5 and 2" combination. Haloperidol blocks D2 receptors to control psychosis and agitation, while lorazepam enhances GABAA transmission to produce rapid sedation, reduce muscle tension, and significantly lower the incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia) caused by haloperidol. (Second-generation IM antipsychotics like olanzapine or ziprasidone are acceptable alternatives, but IM olanzapine must NEVER be combined simultaneously with IM benzodiazepines due to excessive risks of fatal respiratory arrest).

options.text: Application of four-point physical leather restraints alone without any pharmacologic sedation
options.explanation: Physical restraints without chemical sedation are dangerous, leading to intense physical struggling, severe rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia, and sudden cardiac death.

subject: Geriatrics
topic: Delirium vs Dementia Differentiation and Non-Pharmacologic Management
stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted to the medical ward for treatment of a non-severe community-acquired pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone. She has a baseline history of mild vascular dementia for which she lives with her daughter and is fully capable of eating, dressing, and recognizing family members. On her second hospital night, she becomes suddenly agitated, attempts to climb out of bed, and pulls out her peripheral intravenous catheter, screaming that strangers are trying to poison her. On physical examination the following morning, the patient is drowsy and slow to respond. When the physician attempts to engage her, she falls asleep mid-sentence, drifts off topic, and is unable to name the days of the week in reverse order or count backward from 20. Two hours later during afternoon rounds, she is wide awake, hypervigilant, and crying hysterically. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg, heart rate is 88/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Auscultation reveals resolving right lower lobe crackles. A urinary catheter is placed and drains 850 mL of cloudy urine. Complete blood count shows white blood cell count 11,200/mm³, and urinalysis demonstrates 3+ leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, and > 50 WBCs per high-power field. Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach for this patient's acute neurocognitive change?

options.text: Administer scheduled intravenous lorazepam every 6 hours to manage nighttime agitation
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines paradoxically worsen delirium in elderly patients, increase fall risk, and lengthen ICU and hospital stay; they are contraindicated unless delirium is from alcohol withdrawal.

options.text: Reassure the family that this acute deterioration represents the expected natural progression of vascular dementia
options.explanation: Vascular dementia progresses slowly in a stepwise fashion; acute dramatic day-to-night cognitive fluctuations with inattention indicate acute reversible delirium.

options.text: Initiate high-dose oral donepezil and memantine to improve acute cholinergic transmission
options.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors do not treat or reverse acute delirium and can cause bradycardia, syncope, and gastrointestinal adverse effects.

options.text: Place the patient in continuous four-point wrist and ankle restraints to prevent catheter dislodgement
options.explanation: Physical restraints increase agitation, delirium severity, strangulation risk, pressure ulcers, and aspiration; they should be avoided.

options.text: Treat the underlying urinary tract infection, implement non-pharmacologic delirium interventions, and avoid benzodiazepines
options.explanation: This elderly patient has developed ACUTE DELIRIUM superimposed on pre-existing mild dementia. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition that is triggered by an underlying medical condition, infection, or medication. Key features that differentiate delirium from underlying dementia include: (1) Acute onset over hours to days (versus insidious progression over months to years in dementia); (2) Fluctuating course throughout the day (drowsy and inattentive in the morning, hypervigilant and agitated in the afternoon); and (3) Prominent impairment in ATTENTION (inability to recite months or days backward or sustain focus), whereas attention is typically preserved in early-to-moderate dementia. The acute delirium here was precipitated by a combination of hospitalization, acute pneumonia, and a new acute urinary tract infection with urinary retention (draining 850 mL). The cornerstone of delirium management is: (1) Promptly identifying and treating underlying medical triggers (adjusting antibiotics for UTI and relieving urinary retention); and (2) Implementing non-pharmacologic multi-component delirium interventions (reorientation, providing hearing aids and eyeglasses, maintaining day-night circadian light cycles, encouraging early mobility, and involving family members). Crucially, BENZODIAZEPINES SHOULD BE STRICTLY AVOIDED because they paradoxically worsen confusion, increase fall risk, and prolong delirium duration (they are indicated only for delirium caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal).

AVOID BENZODIAZEPINES (paradoxically worsens delirium and prolongs hospitalization; only indicated if alcohol/sedative withdrawal).
